content: In mathematics, a relatively compact subspace (or relatively compact subset) Y of a topological space X is defined as a subset whose closure is compact. This means that the closure of Y, which includes all its limit points, is a compact set. In compact spaces, every subset is relatively compact because closed subsets of compact spaces are themselves compact. This property ensures that any subset of a compact space automatically satisfies the condition of relative compactness. When dealing with metric topologies, or more generally in cases where sequences can be used to test for compactness, the criterion for relative compactness is that any sequence within the subset Y must have a subsequence that converges to a point in the larger space X. This condition is also referred to as pre-compactness or relative boundedness. Several significant theorems provide characterizations of relatively compact subsets, particularly in the context of function spaces. One notable example is the Arzelà-Ascoli theorem, which gives conditions under which a family of functions is relatively compact in the space of continuous functions. Other important cases involve concepts such as uniform integrability and the notion of a normal family in complex analysis, which are used to study the behavior of families of functions under specific conditions. In the geometry of numbers, Mahler's compactness theorem characterizes relatively compact subsets in certain non-compact homogeneous spaces, specifically spaces of lattices. This theorem provides a framework for understanding relative compactness in these specialized mathematical settings. The definition of an almost periodic function F is conceptually tied to the idea that the set of all translates of F forms a relatively compact set. However, this concept must be rigorously defined in terms of the specific topology being used within the relevant mathematical theory.
